name: Longshan culture
title: The story of the Longshan culture

text: About 5,000 years ago, farmers lived along the Yellow River in northern China.
Their culture is named after Longshan, which means “Dragon Mountain”, a town near where its remains were found in 1928.
src: a late Neolithic culture of the middle and lower Yellow River valley in northern China, from about 3000 to 1900 BCE
It is named after the town of Longshan, “Dragon Mountain”, in Zhangqiu, Shandong, near the Chengziya site, found in 1928

text: They grew millet above all, with some rice and wheat.
Pigs gave them most of their meat, and they also kept sheep, goats and dogs.
src: Longshan farmers grew foxtail millet above all, with traces of broomcorn millet, rice and wheat
Pigs were the main source of meat; sheep and goats reached western Henan by 2800 BCE, dogs were eaten

text: They raised silkworms and made a little silk.
Potters used a fast-turning wheel to make shiny black pots so thin they are called egg-shell pottery.
src: Silkworms were raised to make silk on a small scale
highly polished black pottery, also called egg-shell pottery. Its potters used the wheel and made thin-walled vessels with great skill / the quick wheel came into wide use

text: As the number of people grew, about thirty towns were ringed with walls of rammed earth, earth pressed down hard.
A weapon called the dagger-axe shows that fighting became more common.
src: In the 3rd millennium BCE its population grew sharply: towns were walled with rammed earth / some thirty towns are walled with rammed earth
the dagger-axe, a purely military weapon, points to more frequent fighting

text: People heated the shoulder bones of animals to try to learn hidden things, a practice called divination.
src: Longshan people practised divination by heating the shoulder blades of cattle, pigs, sheep and deer

text: Late on, metalworkers made copper tools, rings and bells, leading the way to the Bronze Age.
About 4,000 years ago many big towns were left empty, but in central Henan the culture grew into the Erlitou culture.
src: The late period saw more widespread and skilled making of copper tools, rings and bells, with a few objects of bronze and brass, paving the way for the Bronze Age cultures that followed
Around 2000 BCE its population fell sharply and large settlements were abandoned, except in central Henan, where the culture developed into the Bronze Age Erlitou culture
